reason: The one web listener is kept: one concrete bind address, optional TLS that fails closed, opt-in gzip that never touches the event stream, and a shutdown that ends open streams. Changed: admission is a fixed pipeline inside the listener instead of cordis events, handlers attach as mounts that state each request's class, the route table itself is area A19's and is one such mount, a network bind without TLS is refused unless flagged, and there is no fallback seat or index injection.

Upstream serves a built single-page application from a directory and renders start-up data into its index. The Go host renders pages itself and serves only the files those pages reference, from an embedded file system, with the harness media-type table, nosniff, a build-hash ETag and 404 for every miss.

The launch token exchanged for a signed, audience-bound, HttpOnly, SameSite=Strict cookie is kept, with the durable signing secret. Changed: a token works once and expires, each browser has its own peer and can be signed out, all browsers can be revoked without a restart, and the /connect exchange for API clients is not built because there is no RPC gateway.

The provider exists to keep a credential out of the Electron renderer by passing it over the desktop shell's private channel. The owner removed the desktop application, so there is no shell, no private channel and no second credential path to verify.

The seam is kept as one contract package, dirbrowse, whose only interaction is the server-side browser. The capability union that let a backend be either a native chooser or a browser is gone because only one interaction remains; a remote world may still provide the same interface for its own machine.

The chooser existed to guess at boot whether the operator sits at the host's display and to mount a native or a browse backend accordingly. With one server-side browser there is nothing to choose between, and the guess could not be proven from launch-time signals.

One-level directory listing and single-segment child creation are kept with the same bounds, sorting, link handling and fully-qualified path fence. Added: the Windows hidden attribute, a roots level that lists drives or configured roots, and optional roots enforced through os.Root handles.

A native folder dialog opens on the host machine's display, which a browser user may not be looking at, and the Windows dialog needs a native COM binding that a pure-Go binary cannot carry. The owner's decision on the desktop application already turns native folder dialogs into a host-rendered picker.

Opening a workspace directory in an installed editor, Git client, terminal or file manager is kept, with the fixed catalog, verified launchers, argument lists without a shell, a scrubbed environment and the owner-only rule. Tightened: the route exists only in local mode with a display and outside SSH, the path must lie inside a registered workspace, and operator-defined entries come from config. Icon extraction is not built.

The read-only projection of what is composed in the host is kept and still reads the loader on each call. It gains the supplying layer per entry, rows for plugin processes loaded from local directories with their manifests and grants, an explicit availability flag for presets, a change event and a bounded history of phase changes.

Upstream offers one emit call for caller-selected records to a compiled-in collector. The Go design replaces it with two typed reporting channels, analytics and telemetry, whose events come from a closed catalog, which are off until the user turns them on, have no endpoint compiled in, and attach no account or device identity.

The channel factory built on seven OpenTelemetry SDK packages and a second HTTP client is replaced by one harness exporter on the standard library, as the library specification decided. This area adds that a channel needs a sharing permit, reports each batch's outcome, and drains for three seconds on unload.

The limitation describes the desktop start-up component and its shared owner peer for the desktop lifetime. That component exists only because of the Electron shell, which the Go design does not have, so the limit cannot arise.

The cookie payload carries a random browser id and each id gets its own peer, so one browser can be signed out and only its streams end. Unloading the authentication component still ends every peer, which is ownership working as designed.

A listener on a non-loopback address without TLS is refused at start-up unless the operator sets an explicit insecure flag, which warns at every start and in the UI. On loopback the cookie does not leave the machine. The Secure attribute still follows the listener's own protocol.

The listener owns the rule for the token parameter on every path: only GET on the root is the exchange, and a token parameter on any other request is answered 400 before routing and is never passed to a handler or written to a log.

Nothing infers where the operator sits any more. There is one directory browser, rendered in the page, which works the same for a local browser, a forwarded port and a detached terminal session, so a wrong inference cannot open a dialog on an unattended machine.
The probe for a Linux chooser program on PATH is not built, because no native chooser is started. The directory browser needs no desktop tooling.
The boot-time choice between two interactions is removed. Every client of a host gets the same browser interaction, so no per-connection capability or wire advertisement is needed.

A proxy that presents a loopback authority can no longer cause a native dialog on the host display, because no native dialog exists. The same case for open-in-app is bounded by the rule that only a workspace directory can be opened in a catalog application.
Go exposes the Windows file attributes of a directory entry, so the hidden flag is the dot prefix on every system and also FILE_ATTRIBUTE_HIDDEN on Windows, with no native probe.
The listing has a roots level above the top of a tree. On Windows it lists the drive letters that answer a bounded probe, so a person can cross drives without typing a path.

The browser accepts an optional list of roots in config and performs every listing and creation through an os.Root handle for its root. The specification states that this is a security boundary only when workspace creation honours the same roots, and asks area A07 for that.
The macOS activation problem belongs to a scripted native panel started from a background process. No native panel is started; the picker is part of the page the user is already looking at.
The dependency on Zenity or KDialog is removed with the native backend. The browser interaction, which upstream names as the fallback, is the only interaction.
The Windows child process that drives a COM dialog through a native binding is not built, so a COM refusal or dialog crash has nowhere to occur, and the binary needs no native binding.
The synthesised key press that lets a background process bring its dialog to the foreground is not needed: the harness opens no window of its own on the host.
The contract has a roots level: a listing above the top returns the configured roots, or the drives on Windows, so several roots and drive enumeration are part of the one browser interface.
Content types come from the one harness media-type table that every file-serving path reads, not from a nine-entry starter table, and an unknown extension is served as a download with nosniff.

There is no single-page application and no fallback for unmatched paths. Every page is a route its owner registers explicitly in area A19's route table, which the listener reaches as one mount, and a miss is 404.

An operator can add application entries in a config layer, each with a label and an argument template, next to the embedded catalog. A request can still never name a program; only catalog ids and operator entry ids are accepted.
macOS detection still checks known application directories only. A renamed or moved bundle is not found by the catalog; the operator adds it as a config entry.
justification: A Launch Services query needs a native API, and decision DH-ADR-15 keeps the binary pure Go. Decision DH-ADR-HOST-9 keeps known-path detection and gives the operator-defined entry as the way to add an application the catalog does not find.

reason: Application icons are no better than upstream's and in fact absent: the Go design extracts none and shows a category glyph with the application's name.
justification: Extracting an icon needs a platform helper program or a native API on each system, for a decoration. Decision DH-ADR-HOST-9 drops extraction and states the visible cost; the limit is kept on purpose, not hidden.

reason: Resolution runs on first use and again when the list is asked for after a configured refresh age, so a newly installed application appears without restarting the host. A missing launcher is still re-resolved on the spot.

The inventory raises a change event and keeps a bounded in-memory history of phase changes, so an entry that failed and was removed can still be shown with its reason. The history ends with the process; the log file is the durable record.

Each entry row names the layer that supplied it, read from the loader's ownership index. Mutation stays out of the inventory by decision: composition is changed through settings forms and plugin installation, which other areas own.
The presets part of a snapshot is always present and carries an explicit availability flag, so a reader can tell that no preset registry is composed from an empty roster.

Event selection is no longer free: an event is a Go type declared in a catalog whose fields may only be booleans, integers, duration buckets and strings from a closed set. There is no renderer-to-host transport because the host renders the UI, and the only identity attribute is the anonymous installation id.
The queue for analytics and telemetry records is still memory-only: overflow, a failed request and process exit lose records. The loss is counted and shown in the settings page.
justification: Kept on purpose by decision DH-ADR-HOST-7. A durable outbox would store usage data on disk and would have to be purged when the user withdraws consent; counts of product events do not justify that. A consumer that needs delivery, the session upload, gets a per-batch outcome and keeps its own progress in the session log.

reason: Every channel is bounded by record count and by uncompressed request bytes, because the exporter owns the encoder and knows each record's size. An ordinary channel defaults to one million bytes per request and cannot exceed four million.

There are no caller-selected free strings to redact: the catalog refuses an event type with a free-text field at start-up. Disclosure and consent are decided in one place, the sharing gate, whose permit the reporter needs before it creates a channel.

The certificate and key are re-read when the files change, so a renewed certificate is served to the next handshake without a restart, and a bad replacement keeps the last good pair. Issuing and renewing certificates stays with the operator, as upstream decided.

The source check and the route class are steps of the listener itself and cannot be unmounted, so an anonymous route is never reachable without the Host and origin checks. Only the credential lookup and the non-owner policy are answered by other components.

The settings a deployment tunes are config fields with defaults: header read timeout, idle timeout, header size and shutdown grace, with write deadlines set per route. Go takes the accept backlog from the operating system's limit, so there is no harness constant to expose.

Consent is enforced by the factory: a channel cannot be created without a sharing permit and closes without a drain when the permit ends. The shutdown deadline has a default. Redaction and field selection stay with the consumer, and resource identity is evaluated lazily at the first accepted record.

The channel stays memory-only, but it now reports every batch as delivered, failed, dropped or cancelled with the sequence range it covered. A consumer with a durable source, the session upload that reads the session log, resumes after the last delivered record, so loss in the channel no longer means loss of the upload.
There is one channel type and it batches by count and by bytes, so a consumer no longer has to pick event and batch sizes that happen to fit the collector's request limit.

The first-answer-wins credential lookup is kept as the typed bail key listen.Authenticate: cookie and audience in, peer out. The source check and the class of a request are steps of the listener and no longer part of the event, and what a non-owner may do is decided afterwards by area A19's access.Decide.

Upstream collects entry URLs from every credential provider through an event. The Go host has one credential scheme, so the launch component calls the authentication service directly for a fresh one-time URL, then prints it or hands it to the browser.

The event gathers start-up data rows to render into the single-page application's index. Server-rendered pages need no injection: the page shell renders start-up data from host state for the admitted peer.

The waterfall let any listener own a response before routing and admission; its one shipped use was the token exchange. The exchange is now a fixed step of the listener's admission pipeline and no middleware runs before admission.

The waterfall existed so that the token plugin could enforce one socket per API peer and revoke its credential on close. API peers are not built, and a WebSocket is an ordinary stream request of a mount: admitted like any other request, exempt from compression and the write timeout, and ended when the listener's Done channel closes.
The schema's one field is an in-memory function that reads the desktop shell's private credential. With no desktop application there is no component to configure.
cookieMaxAgeDays becomes auth.Config.CookieMaxAge with the same 30-day default and one-day minimum; LaunchTokenTTL is added for one-time tokens.
maxEntries becomes dirbrowse.Config.MaxEntries with the same default of 1,000; Roots is added to scope what may be listed and created.
The schema's one field points at the built front end's index file on disk. Assets are embedded in the binary, so the assets component has no config and nothing on disk to point at.

probeTimeoutMs and launchWatchMs become openpath.Config.ProbeTimeout and LaunchWatch, now with defaults. iconTimeoutMs has no counterpart because icons are not extracted. Enabled, RefreshAfter and operator-defined Apps are added.

The queue, batch, interval and timeout fields become report.Config with the same count defaults, plus a byte bound and a three-second drain. The endpoint default is empty instead of the upstream vendor's collector, the channel header becomes a list of credential references, and each kind has its own live Enabled field that defaults to false.

host, port, tls and the three compression fields become listen.Config with the same meaning: one address literal, the unspecified address refused, TLS as a pair, compression off by default. Added: the explicit insecure-remote flag, trusted hosts, a public URL, timeouts and a shutdown grace period.

ctx.directoryPicker becomes the service key dirbrowse.Key with interface dirbrowse.Service (List and CreateDirectory). The capability method that told a consumer which interaction a backend offers is gone because there is one interaction.

ctx.otel becomes the service key otlplog.Key with interface otlplog.Service. Its two factory methods for ordinary and session-log channels become one NewChannel that takes a sharing permit and options, and providing the service still allocates nothing.

ctx.productTelemetry.emit becomes the service key report.Key with interface report.Reporter, whose two methods take events declared in a closed catalog under the analytics or telemetry kind and drop them when that kind has no permit.

ctx.webServer is split in two. The socket's facts (Origin, Secure, Mode, Ready, Done) and the Mount call that attaches a handler behind the admission pipeline become the service key listen.Key with interface listen.Listener. Registering a UI route is area A19's web.Key, which mounts its table on the listener. registerFallback, readResource and the index rendering methods have no counterpart.

Kept: every request is authenticated by a signed, audience-bound cookie obtained from a random launch token, after the Host and origin checks, with a durable signing secret so that a restart does not sign browsers out. Changed after reading the note: the token is one-time and short-lived instead of valid for the process lifetime, each browser has its own peer, sign-out and revoke-all exist, and the /connect handshake the note delegates to is not built.

Kept as written: one base element per page, references and the token redirect relative to the document, no configured base URL and no forwarded-prefix header as a routing input, so one binary works at the origin root and under a prefix-stripping proxy. The rule for the page shell is requested from area C1; the redirect and the proxy scenario are this area's.

Kept as written: one concrete IPv4 or IPv6 literal, loopback by default, the unspecified address refused in every spelling at load, the bind literal accepted as Host on any port, every other name only from trusted hosts, and a public URL required for a zoned non-loopback bind. The Go parser is net/netip and the listener is opened from the parsed value.

Kept: optional TLS on the one listener from a certificate and key file, bad material fails start-up with no fallback to HTTP, the listener's own protocol decides the Secure attribute, and the harness issues no certificate. Changed: a non-loopback listener without TLS is refused unless an explicit flag is set, where upstream warns, and replaced certificate files are picked up without a restart.

Kept: caller-owned independent channels, a request bounded by uncompressed bytes as well as count, one event per record, an oversized record rejected whole with one diagnostic and never truncated, one request in flight. Changed: the byte bound applies to every channel, a record is encoded once, the request deadline really ends the request, and each batch reports its outcome. The record shape for session events is area A06's.

title: Admission is a fixed pipeline inside the listener; the credential lookup is its only extension point
A network listener needs TLS or an explicit flag, and remote mode switches host-local actions off
Launch tokens are one-time, sessions are per browser, and a second dsh asks the running host to open a new link
Owner authority is never handed to a caller, never readable from disk, and refused to a process the host started for the model
Peer rule: a process in an untrusted tree is refused on the control endpoint, the token exchange and a required request before any credential is read
Linux: a command run for the model cannot make itself the owner
macOS: the same attempt under Seatbelt
Windows: the same attempt under the restricted token
No desktop credential provider and no API-client handshake on the listener
One sharing gate: every sender is registered, has its own setting, and needs a permit; one off-switch wins
No collector is compiled in; analytics and telemetry are closed catalogs with no account or device identity
Channels stay memory-only and report every batch's outcome
One server-side directory browser; no native chooser and no boot-time guess
The host opens only workspace directories, only in catalog or operator-defined applications, only for a local owner
A fatal failure prints one diagnostic and leaves one local, bounded report
The plugin inventory is a read-only projection that names layers and plugin processes
The listener: one address, optional TLS, admission-gated mounts, embedded assets, a shutdown that ends streams
A browser is admitted by source, then by a cookie from a launch token, and arrives as a peer
Running dsh shows the UI, and running it again reuses the host
Nothing leaves the machine by default, each kind has a visible setting, and one switch stops all of them
One exporter sends OpenTelemetry log records, bounded by bytes, for whoever holds a permit
Other areas report product and operational events through two typed channels
A host that cannot continue says why once and leaves a report
The owner chooses a directory of the host machine from the browser
A local owner opens a workspace directory in an editor, terminal or file manager on the host
The host reports what is composed in it, including plugin directories and their grants
Bind address table: loopback spellings accepted, unspecified addresses and host names refused
TLS material fails closed at start and a replaced pair is picked up
A network bind without TLS is refused unless the insecure flag is set; local and remote mode
Mounts: overlapping prefixes refused, deny and a panicking classifier answer 403, streams wait for readiness
Unloading the listener ends open streams and WebSocket connections within the grace period
Embedded assets: containment, media types, revalidation and misses
Compression is off by default and never applied to a stream, an asset or a range response
Connection limits are enforced and a panicking handler does not stop the listener
Source check table for Host, Origin and Sec-Fetch-Site on every method, before any credential
The launch token exchange works once, expires, and a token parameter elsewhere is rejected and never logged
Cookie forgery, audience, expiry and the Secure attribute; stale cookies for another port are expired
One peer per browser; sign-out and revoke-all end the right streams; cookies survive a restart
Class table: required needs a peer, anonymous reads no cookie, callback allows cross-site, a peer's context ends on sign-out
Without the authentication component required requests answer 503; no connect route and no desktop cookie exist
Print and open decision table, and a launcher that gets one argument and a scrubbed environment
Runtime record and control endpoint: reuse of a live host, replacement of a stale record, cleanup on unload
A fresh home in every shipped profile makes no outbound request and no name lookup beyond the model provider
The off-switch, by config and by environment variable, silences every sender and cancels the request in flight
Every sharing-purpose client belongs to a registered sender; no HTTP client is built outside egress
A channel needs a permit, closes without a drain when it ends, and reports each batch's outcome
The event catalog refuses free text; the resource is exact; no installation id before the first accepted record
Analytics and telemetry are switched independently and an undeclared event is refused
A fatal failure prints one diagnostic, writes a complete report with secrets redacted, releases and exits non-zero
Crash file set first and removed on clean exit; reports pruned to ten; unclean-exit notice at the next start
Directory listing: bounds, order, links, hidden flags, the path fence, roots and cancellation
Directory creation rules with typed errors, and the roots level
Open-in-app locality table: no routes in remote mode, under SSH or without a display; a non-owner is refused; no process starts
Only a workspace directory and a known application start a launcher, as an argument list with a scrubbed environment
An inventory snapshot shows layer, phase, diagnostic and history, and the service cannot mutate
Plugin process rows and the change event, with a fake plugin host
A real browser is signed in by dsh, a second dsh reuses the host, and other origins are refused
A network listener refuses plain HTTP, serves TLS, works behind a path prefix, and picks up a new certificate
Nothing reaches the network by default, and the off-switch is shown locked by the environment
A host that dies leaves a readable report on each operating system
Choosing a directory of the host machine, at the machine and away from it
Opening a workspace in an application works at the machine and is absent away from it
The exporter delivers to a real collector, acknowledges each batch, and stops at the switch
Opting in to analytics sends exactly the declared catalog and nothing else
The inventory shows a real plugin process from a local directory
